_readme: Tier-1 reskins for the CUS and PRD events (Addendum B §3.1). Same format,
same rules and same register as industry/reskins.json — keyed by event id,
then by industry code, each string replacing GameEvent.text wholesale.
WHY A SECOND FILE: reskins.json is the first pass across every category.
These twelve are the events where the PRODUCT ITSELF is in the text, which is
the tier that breaks immersion hardest — a food company reading about its
engineers, a toy company reading about its login screen. Split so the two
passes can be revised independently.
THE BAR (Addendum B §3.2): a reskin is not flavour. Each one turns the same
mechanical event into a different lesson — FOOD's grandma is about ordering-
flow accessibility, FASHION's about size charts, PET's about packaging. Same
choices, same effects, same authored outcome; different thing learned.
RULES FOR ADDING TO THIS FILE
1. Never change what the situation MEANS. The choices are shared across all
twelve industries and their outcomes are unchanged — a rewrite that
shifts the problem makes the choices answer a different question.
2. Preserve every figure the choices depend on. E-CUS-002 stays 25%,
E-CUS-007 stays 2S/yr. An event whose numbers cannot survive the rewrite
does not get one.
3. Tokens {topItem} / {newestItem} / {company} resolve at draw time and fall
back to a generic noun, so every sentence has to read correctly with the
fallback substituted.
4. Real words only (Brand Law 6). Wholesale, sell-through, batch record,
tooling, screen reader. No invented units.
5. No real companies, platforms or people. "the platform", "a big-box
retailer", "a national chain".
6. Same register as the base text: terse, second person, dry, present tense.

E-CUS-002.CONTENT: One sponsor wants an entire series built around them, with script approval. Worth 25% of annual revenue.
E-CUS-002.FASHION: A department store wants an exclusive capsule in their colours, delivered in their window. Worth 25% of annual revenue.
E-CUS-002.GAMING: One platform wants a timed exclusive with the features they specify. Worth 25% of annual revenue.
E-CUS-002.FITNESS: A corporate wellness programme wants your classes on their campus, on their schedule, under their branding. Worth 25% of annual revenue.

E-CUS-002.PET: A veterinary chain wants a clinic-only formula with their name beside yours on the bag. Worth 25% of annual revenue.

E-PRD-007.FOOD: The kitchen runs on workarounds: prep nobody wrote down, a walk-in stacked by memory, one person who knows where everything is. Rebuild the whole system over a quarter, or keep duct-taping.
E-PRD-007.ECOM: The bin layout, the SKU numbering and the returns process were all improvised in week three and never revisited. Rebuild them over a quarter, or keep duct-taping.
E-PRD-007.TECH: Engineering wants a quarter with no features to rebuild the foundation. The alternative is more duct tape.
E-PRD-007.CONTENT: Your project files, your archive and your upload process are a system only you can navigate. Stop publishing for a quarter and rebuild it, or keep duct-taping.
E-PRD-007.FASHION: Every pattern, grading and supplier spec lives in one spreadsheet and one person's head. Stop for a quarter and rebuild it, or keep duct-taping.
E-PRD-007.GAMING: The build takes forty minutes and breaks weekly. Stop content for a quarter and fix the engine underneath, or keep duct-taping.
E-PRD-007.FITNESS: The timetable, the memberships and the billing are three systems that don't talk to each other. Rebuild them over a quarter, or keep duct-taping.
E-PRD-007.BEAUTY: Your formulas, batch records and stability data are in three formats and one notebook. Rebuild the records over a quarter, or keep duct-taping.
E-PRD-007.EDTECH: The platform was built for one class and is now carrying forty schools. Stop shipping lessons for a term and rebuild it, or keep duct-taping.
E-PRD-007.SUSTAIN: Your carbon accounting is a spreadsheet of hand-typed factors, and you publish claims off it. Rebuild it properly over a quarter, or keep duct-taping.
E-PRD-007.TOYS: The moulds, the parts lists and the safety files have been patched every production run since the first one. Rebuild them over a quarter, or keep duct-taping.
E-PRD-007.PET: Your recipes, batch records and label claims are patched together, and the regulator can ask for any of them. Rebuild over a quarter, or keep duct-taping.

E-PRD-012.FOOD: The dish you opened with — the one on the sign outside — loses money every month it stays on the menu.
E-PRD-012.ECOM: The first product you ever listed loses money every month. It is still the one customers mention.
E-PRD-012.TECH: The first thing you ever shipped loses money every month, and a few hundred customers are still running it.
E-PRD-012.CONTENT: The series that built the channel loses money every month. It is also the reason anyone knows your name.
E-PRD-012.FASHION: The piece you started with loses money every season. It is on every press page you have.
E-PRD-012.GAMING: Your first game loses money every month in servers and support. It is still where new players find you.
E-PRD-012.FITNESS: The class you opened with is half empty and costs more than it takes. Your oldest members are in it.
E-PRD-012.BEAUTY: The product that launched the brand loses money every month. Every article written about you names it.
E-PRD-012.EDTECH: The first course you built loses money every term. It is the one schools trial you with.
E-PRD-012.SUSTAIN: The product you founded the company to make loses money every month. It is the entire pitch.
E-PRD-012.TOYS: The toy that started all of this loses money every production run, and its face is on the packaging of everything else.
E-PRD-012.PET: The first formula you ever bagged loses money every month. Your oldest customers feed nothing else.

E-CUS-006.FOOD: An elderly regular wrote you a paper letter: she can't read {topItem} on the new menu board, and the QR-code-only ordering means she hasn't ordered it in a month.
E-CUS-006.ECOM: A paper letter, forwarded from your fulfilment centre: a 78-year-old customer reached checkout four times and gave up four times. She included the printed screenshots.
E-CUS-006.TECH: A paper letter about {topItem}: "My grandson set it up. Then he went home." She has been paying for three months and cannot log in.
E-CUS-006.CONTENT: A paper letter, forwarded by the platform: she watches every week with the captions on, the captions are auto-generated and wrong, and she has been guessing for a year.
E-CUS-006.FASHION: A handwritten letter: she bought {topItem} for her granddaughter, guessed the size from the photos, and guessed wrong. Your size chart is a lifestyle image.
E-CUS-006.GAMING: A letter from a 74-year-old player — yes, of {topItem}. The update moved the settings menu and she can't find text scaling anymore. She has played since launch.
E-CUS-006.FITNESS: A member since month one wrote you a letter: the new class-booking app has locked her out of the Tuesday session she has attended for two years.
E-CUS-006.BEAUTY: A paper letter in careful handwriting: the ingredient list on the back of {topItem} is grey, six point, and she needs to know what is in it before she puts it on her face.
E-CUS-006.EDTECH: A retired teacher wrote you a paper letter: she bought {topItem} to keep sharp, and the onboarding assumes she knows what a "workspace" is. She reached lesson two.
E-CUS-006.SUSTAIN: A letter from an 81-year-old who wants to do the right thing: your take-back scheme begins with scanning a code, and she does not own a phone that can.
E-CUS-006.TOYS: A grandmother writes: getting {newestItem} out of its box took forty minutes and a pair of kitchen scissors, and the child watched the whole performance.
E-CUS-006.PET: A letter with a photograph of her cat: she can't open {topItem}'s child-proof lid with her arthritis, and the vet says it is the right food for him.

E-PRD-004.FOOD: Half your volume is people buying the sauce by the jar and never sitting down. You built a restaurant.
E-PRD-004.ECOM: Half of {topItem}'s orders ship to an address that isn't the buyer's. You built a product; people are buying a gift.
E-PRD-004.TECH: Customers are running {topItem} as the backbone of a workflow you never built it for, and paying for the larger plan to do it.
E-PRD-004.CONTENT: The clips are outperforming the show, and the sponsors are buying the clips.
E-PRD-004.FASHION: The piece you cut for evening is selling as workwear, in the two most boring colours you offered.
E-PRD-004.GAMING: Players have turned the level editor into the game. The campaign is barely touched.
E-PRD-004.FITNESS: Half your members come for the twenty minutes after class, not the class.
E-PRD-004.BEAUTY: The primer is selling as a hand cream, and it costs more per unit than a hand cream has any business costing.
E-PRD-004.EDTECH: Teachers are using the student course as their own lesson planner and paying for seats they never assign.
E-PRD-004.SUSTAIN: Businesses are buying your consumer product by the pallet for their own operations, and asking for invoices you don't issue.
E-PRD-004.TOYS: Adults are buying {topItem} for themselves. The reviews are written by collectors, not parents.
E-PRD-004.PET: Groomers are buying the shampoo by the case and decanting it. It is priced for one dog, not forty.

E-PRD-009.FOOD: An audit finds the dining room, the menu and the ordering app all exclude people with disabilities. The step at the door is the least of it.
E-PRD-009.ECOM: An accessibility audit finds a screen reader cannot complete a purchase on your site. Not slowly — at all.
E-PRD-009.TECH: An audit finds {topItem} unusable with a screen reader, and keyboard navigation stops dead at the login form.
E-PRD-009.CONTENT: An audit finds no usable captions, no transcripts, and flashing sequences with no warning on them.
E-PRD-009.FASHION: An audit finds nothing you make can be fastened one-handed, and every product photo on the site has no alt text.
E-PRD-009.GAMING: An audit finds no colourblind mode, no remappable controls, and subtitles nobody can resize.
E-PRD-009.FITNESS: An audit finds not one class on the timetable can be taken seated, and the accessible changing room is where you keep stock.
E-PRD-009.BEAUTY: An audit finds your packaging needs two hands and a fingernail, and your shade names mean nothing to a customer who can't see the swatch.
E-PRD-009.EDTECH: An audit finds the course fails every screen reader and every dyslexic student. Schools are legally obliged to care.
E-PRD-009.SUSTAIN: An audit finds the refill system is unusable by anyone who can't lift and pour eight kilos.
E-PRD-009.TOYS: An audit finds nothing in the range is playable by a child who can't grip with both hands, and every instruction is a wordless diagram.
E-PRD-009.PET: An audit finds your bags need scissors and two hands. A guide-dog owner has been writing to you about it for a year.
